courseTitle: Swedish for YKI: A1 to B1 Late-August Course
description: An 84-lesson Swedish course organized into A1, A2, and B1 sections, designed for steady preparation toward a late-August 2026 YKI-style target with daily retrieval practice, weekly checkpoints, and skill-balanced tasks.
examGoal: Target: practical B1-level Swedish for reading, listening, speaking, and writing in citizenship-oriented YKI preparation.
targetWindow: Late August 2026 (assumption based on your note; roadmap runs through August 30, 2026).
studyMethod: Use six study days per week and keep one lighter review/rest day.
Review each new lesson on D+1, D+3, and D+7 to force retrieval.
Spend at least 15 minutes per day on speaking aloud, not only reading silently.
Do one timed production task every week from the start and one full mock block in the B1 stage.
testWeekAdvice: In the final week, reduce new vocabulary and prioritize stability, sleep, and short mixed-skill review.
Keep one reusable structure ready for greeting, narration, opinion, comparison, problem-solving, and formal messages.
If you miss one detail in listening or reading, recover to the main point instead of freezing.
legacySources: Analyzed class notes from Apr 15 to May 9, 2026, plus Learn Swedish Lab reading extracts, the Swedish A1-A2 tutorial, and a teacher-led lesson expansion from May 18, 2026

levels.title: A1 Foundations

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: Swedish often says “Jag mår bra” for “I am fine.” Literally it means “I feel well,” so do not replace it with “Jag är bra.”
A short answer is common in everyday speech: “Bra, tack.” You can also continue with “Och du?” to keep the conversation going.

sections.heading: Class note pronunciation clinic
content: Your notes confirm that the first big A1 hurdle is vowel control. Focus on the shape of your mouth, not only the spelling, because Swedish changes meaning quickly when vowel quality changes.
The strongest beginner pairs in your notes are tack / tak, kaffe / kafé, ful / full, and gratis / grattis. These are good reminders that vowel length and consonant length matter together.

legacyCompanion.title: Saying your name and where you are from
legacyCompanion.goal: Introduce yourself, say your name, and tell someone where you are from.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: Today you build your first self-introduction in Swedish: your name, your country, and a simple question back to the other person.
By the end of the lesson you should be able to give a short three-line introduction about yourself without reading.

table.Example Swedish: Jag kommer från Indien. Och du?
table.Example English: I come from India. And you?

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: “Jag heter” means “my name is.” To say where you are from, use “Jag kommer från ...” or “Jag är från ...” in simple beginner speech.
Use “Jag bor i ...” for the place where you live now. A beginner self-introduction can combine all three patterns: name, country, and city.

legacyCompanion.title: Classroom phrases and polite requests
legacyCompanion.goal: Use basic classroom Swedish to ask for repetition, help, and clarification.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: This lesson gives you survival Swedish for learning: asking someone to repeat, saying you do not understand, and asking what a word means.
These phrases are useful in class, at work, and anytime you need someone to slow down or explain something.

table.Example English: What does that mean in English?
Excuse me, can you help me?
Can you speak more slowly, please?

table.English: how do you say ... in Swedish?
table.Example English: How do you say “table” in Swedish?

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: “Kan du ...?” means “Can you ...?” and is a useful polite frame for requests. “Jag förstår inte” means “I do not understand.”
When you ask about language, “på svenska” means “in Swedish” and “på engelska” means “in English.”

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.english: Do you understand?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.english: Not really. Can you repeat?

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.english: Of course.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.english: Thanks! What does “från” mean?

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.english: It means “from”.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Bra, tack. Kan du tala långsammare också?
dialogue.english: Good, thanks. Can you speak more slowly too?

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Practice “Jag förstår inte” without translating in your head.
Ask for repetition politely three times.
Choose one Swedish word and ask what it means.
Read the dialogue with a pause after each line.

sections.heading: Extra practice ideas
list: Ask one question with “Vad betyder det?” and another with “Hur säger man ... på svenska?”.
Practice one polite request starting with “Ursäkta ...”.
Role-play a short teacher-student exchange with a friend or by yourself.

items: how do you say ... in Swedish?
You need someone to repeat a sentence.
You want the speaker to slow down.
You want to know the Swedish word for “book”.

legacyResources.summary: This lesson now teaches classroom phrases as survival language, not isolated formulas, so the learner can keep a conversation going even when they miss something.

sections.heading: Teaching focus
content: Treat these phrases as control tools. A beginner does not need to understand everything immediately; they need to know how to slow the conversation down, ask for repetition, and signal confusion politely.
Practice each phrase with a clear purpose: asking someone to repeat, asking what a word means, asking for help, and thanking the other person after they help you.

sections.heading: Common mistakes to watch
list: Do not memorize only the English meaning. Pair each phrase with a real situation, such as class, a shop, or a phone call.
Say the whole chunk, not just one word. Kan du hjälpa mig? is much stronger than only saying Hjälp.
Repeat the phrases aloud until they feel automatic, because these are emergency expressions you need quickly.

sections.heading: Guided practice
list: Say three repair phrases in a row: Kan du säga det igen? Jag förstår inte. Kan du hjälpa mig?
Roleplay a mini-dialogue where you do not hear a word and ask for clarification politely.
Write two short classroom questions and answer them aloud.

legacyCompanion.goal: Count from 0 to 20, say your age, and read simple numbers aloud.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: Today you train Swedish numbers so you can say your age and begin hearing number patterns clearly.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: To say your age, Swedish uses “Jag är ... år.” The word “år” means “years old” in this context.
Phone numbers are usually read digit by digit. Practice them slowly first and then at a more natural speed.

sections.heading: Teaching focus
content: Numbers are not only vocabulary; they are listening training. Learners often know the numbers on paper but freeze when they hear them quickly. Move between reading, hearing, and saying them.
Work especially with age and phone numbers, because those force you to pronounce digits clearly one by one and notice Swedish rhythm.

sections.heading: Common mistakes to watch
list: Do not rush teen numbers. Check carefully that you hear and say them distinctly.
When giving a phone number, say the digits clearly in groups instead of one long stream.
Mix recognition and production: first listen and identify, then say your own examples.

legacyCompanion.title: Verb är: to be

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: This lesson gives you one of the most important verbs in Swedish so you can describe identity, location, and simple facts.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: The present form is “är” for all persons: jag är, du är, vi är. Swedish does not change it like English does with am / is / are.

sections.heading: Teaching focus
content: A beginner should overlearn är because it appears everywhere: names, nationality, feelings, descriptions, and simple classification. The goal is fast accurate use, not grammar theory alone.
Practice both statements and questions side by side. When the learner can switch between Du är trött. and Är du trött? the structure starts to become active.

sections.heading: Common mistakes to watch
list: Do not confuse Jag är bra with Jag mår bra. Use är for identity or description, and mår for how you feel.
Keep the word order stable when forming questions with är.
Avoid overtranslating from English. Use short natural Swedish sentences first.

sections.heading: Guided practice
list: Make five sentences with är about yourself, your city, and your family.

sections.heading: Teaching focus
content: For early Swedish, sentence control matters more than long vocabulary lists. The learner should feel that a simple sentence has a dependable skeleton: subject first, verb second, then the rest.

sections.heading: Common mistakes to watch

Read your sentences aloud, because spoken rhythm often shows whether the order feels natural.

sections.heading: Teaching focus
content: Likes and dislikes are high-value speaking material because they connect easily to food, hobbies, studies, places, and people. The learner should practice full opinion sentences, not just gillar or gillar inte.
A strong beginner pattern is opinion plus reason: Jag gillar kaffe eftersom det är gott. That turns a basic A1 answer into a more useful A2-style response.

sections.heading: Common mistakes to watch
list: Do not answer only with Ja or Nej when the topic is personal preference.
Remember that gillar often needs an object: Jag gillar musik, not only Jag gillar.
Use one reason word such as eftersom to make the answer more informative.

list: Give three likes and three dislikes with short reasons.

sections.heading: Adverb slot from class
content: Your notes repeat the same high-value rule: inte, också, alltid, ofta, sällan, and aldrig sit in the same adverbial slot. That is why “Jag vill inte läsa”, “Jag vill också läsa”, and “Jag läser ofta hemma” follow parallel patterns.

table.Swedish: Jag vill också köpa en banan.
table.English: I also want to buy a banana.

table.Swedish: Jag går alltid på gymmet efter jobbet.
table.English: I always go to the gym after work.

vocabulary.exampleEnglish: I do not like Anna either.

legacyCompanion.title: Modal verbs
legacyCompanion.goal: Use can, must, want to, and may in simple statements.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: Modal verbs let you speak about ability, obligation, and desire, which makes your Swedish much more functional.

table.Example English: I can speak a little Swedish.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: After a modal verb like “kan”, “vill”, or “måste”, the next verb stays in the infinitive: “Jag kan tala.” “Jag vill gå.”

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.english: Can you help me?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Ja, men jag måste gå snart.
dialogue.english: Yes, but I have to go soon.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.swedish: Får jag fråga en sak först?
dialogue.english: May I ask one thing first?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.english: Yes, of course.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Make one sentence with each modal verb.

Read the dialogue and emphasize the modal verbs.

legacyResources.summary: This lesson now strengthens modal verbs as conversation tools for ability, necessity, permission, and desire rather than as isolated grammar labels.

sections.heading: Teaching focus
content: Modal verbs unlock practical communication quickly. With kan, vill, måste, and får, learners can handle many real needs even with limited vocabulary.
The key teaching point is chunking: modal plus infinitive. Repeat the pattern often until it feels automatic.

sections.heading: Common mistakes to watch
list: Do not forget the second verb after the modal when the meaning needs one.
Separate the meanings clearly: can, want, must, and may are not interchangeable.
Use personal examples so the verbs feel useful, not abstract.

sections.heading: Guided practice
list: Say three things you can do, three things you want to do, and two things you must do.
Ask another person what they can or want to do.
Make one polite permission question with får.

vocabulary.exampleEnglish: I do not have the energy to cook today.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: A practical beginner future form is “ska” + infinitive: “Jag ska studera.” It often means “am going to.”

dialogue.speaker: B

sections.heading: Teaching focus
content: Future language becomes useful when it answers three questions at once: what, when, and why. Even a simple ska sentence becomes stronger with one time phrase and one detail.

sections.heading: Common mistakes to watch
list: Do not stop at Jag ska ... with no completion. Finish the action clearly.
Add a time phrase such as ikväll, imorgon, or nästa vecka whenever possible.
Keep word order stable even when the time phrase comes first.

sections.heading: Guided practice

legacyCompanion.title: Reading simple texts
legacyCompanion.goal: Read short beginner texts and identify the main idea.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: Today is about reading tolerance: understanding enough without translating every single word.

table.Example Swedish: Det finns ett okänt ord här.
table.Example English: There is an unknown word here.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: When reading, focus on known anchors such as names, places, time words, and common verbs before worrying about every detail.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.english: Do you understand the text?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Inte varje ord, men jag förstår huvudidén.
dialogue.english: Not every word, but I understand the main idea.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.english: Good. What is the heading?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Den handlar om en familj i Stockholm.
dialogue.english: It is about a family in Stockholm.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Read a short section without stopping at every unknown word.
Find the topic, place, and time in the text.
Write one English sentence about the main idea.
Read the dialogue and keep a calm reading pace.

legacyResources.summary: This reading lesson now teaches strategy: find the main idea, catch familiar anchors, and tolerate unknown words without stopping every line.

sections.heading: Teaching focus
content: A strong beginner reader does not translate everything. They identify topic, people, place, time, and repeated key words, then build the general meaning from those anchors.
Short texts become valuable when learners reread them with different purposes: first overall meaning, then details, then useful sentence patterns to reuse in their own writing.

sections.heading: Common mistakes to watch
list: Do not stop for every unknown word. First ask whether the whole sentence is still understandable.
Avoid translating word by word when the text is clearly about a familiar topic.
After reading, always summarize in simple Swedish or English to prove comprehension.

sections.heading: Guided practice
list: Read a short text once for the general topic and once for details.
Underline the words that tell you who, where, and when.
Retell the text in three simple Swedish sentences.

sections.heading: Balansen (Textbook page 52)
content: Marias jobb är inte välbetalt men det är roligt. “Man presterar inte om man inte gillar jobbet”, brukar hon säga. Hon tycker också att hennes mentala hälsa är viktig och därför vill hon inte ha ett stressigt jobb. Hon är nöjd med sitt trygga jobb på en statlig myndighet och hon lär sina barn att pengar inte kan köpa allt i livet. Maria brukar säga att hennes man Peter är arbetsnarkoman eftersom han inte slutar med jobbet när han kommer hem. På sitt tidigare jobb hade han en giftig arbetsmiljö så han blev tvungen att säga upp sig. Efter detta startade han eget och därför jobbar han så mycket. Det är inte lätt att vara entreprenör! Han tänker på jobbet hela tiden. Maria tycker att det inte är bra för hälsan. “Det var bättre när han var arbetslös”, säger hon till Lena.

sections.heading: Teaching focus
content: Beginner listening improves when learners predict the topic before listening and then hunt for key information such as names, times, places, numbers, and feelings.
A useful sequence is listen once for the big picture, listen again for details, and only then check exact wording if necessary.

sections.heading: Common mistakes to watch
list: Do not panic when you miss one word. Keep listening for the next clear clue.
Avoid turning listening into reading in your head. Train your ear to catch sound chunks.
Use very short repeats rather than replaying the whole audio without purpose.

sections.heading: Guided practice

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: Swedish often says “Jag mår bra” for “I am fine.” Literally it means “I feel well,” so do not replace it with “Jag är bra.”
A short answer is common in everyday speech: “Bra, tack.” You can also continue with “Och du?” to keep the conversation going.

legacyResources.summary: Your Apr 15 notes deepen the opening lesson with vowel training, sound harmony, and the most common Swedish sound-change patterns.

sections.heading: Class note pronunciation clinic
content: Your notes confirm that the first big A1 hurdle is vowel control. Focus on the shape of your mouth, not only the spelling, because Swedish changes meaning quickly when vowel quality changes.
The strongest beginner pairs in your notes are tack / tak, kaffe / kafé, ful / full, and gratis / grattis. These are good reminders that vowel length and consonant length matter together.

legacyCompanion.title: Classroom phrases and polite requests
legacyCompanion.goal: Use basic classroom Swedish to ask for repetition, help, and clarification.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: This lesson gives you survival Swedish for learning: asking someone to repeat, saying you do not understand, and asking what a word means.
These phrases are useful in class, at work, and anytime you need someone to slow down or explain something.

table.Example English: What does that mean in English?
Excuse me, can you help me?
Can you speak more slowly, please?

table.English: how do you say ... in Swedish?
table.Example English: How do you say “table” in Swedish?

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: “Kan du ...?” means “Can you ...?” and is a useful polite frame for requests. “Jag förstår inte” means “I do not understand.”
When you ask about language, “på svenska” means “in Swedish” and “på engelska” means “in English.”

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.english: Do you understand?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.english: Not really. Can you repeat?

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.english: Of course.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.english: Thanks! What does “från” mean?

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.english: It means “from”.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Bra, tack. Kan du tala långsammare också?
dialogue.english: Good, thanks. Can you speak more slowly too?

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Practice “Jag förstår inte” without translating in your head.
Ask for repetition politely three times.
Choose one Swedish word and ask what it means.
Read the dialogue with a pause after each line.

sections.heading: Extra practice ideas
list: Ask one question with “Vad betyder det?” and another with “Hur säger man ... på svenska?”.
Practice one polite request starting with “Ursäkta ...”.
Role-play a short teacher-student exchange with a friend or by yourself.

items: how do you say ... in Swedish?
You need someone to repeat a sentence.
You want the speaker to slow down.
You want to know the Swedish word for “book”.

legacyResources.summary: This lesson now teaches classroom phrases as survival language, not isolated formulas, so the learner can keep a conversation going even when they miss something.

sections.heading: Teaching focus
content: Treat these phrases as control tools. A beginner does not need to understand everything immediately; they need to know how to slow the conversation down, ask for repetition, and signal confusion politely.
Practice each phrase with a clear purpose: asking someone to repeat, asking what a word means, asking for help, and thanking the other person after they help you.

sections.heading: Common mistakes to watch
list: Do not memorize only the English meaning. Pair each phrase with a real situation, such as class, a shop, or a phone call.
Say the whole chunk, not just one word. Kan du hjälpa mig? is much stronger than only saying Hjälp.
Repeat the phrases aloud until they feel automatic, because these are emergency expressions you need quickly.

sections.heading: Guided practice
list: Say three repair phrases in a row: Kan du säga det igen? Jag förstår inte. Kan du hjälpa mig?
Roleplay a mini-dialogue where you do not hear a word and ask for clarification politely.
Write two short classroom questions and answer them aloud.

legacyCompanion.goal: Count from 0 to 20, say your age, and read simple numbers aloud.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: Today you train Swedish numbers so you can say your age and begin hearing number patterns clearly.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: To say your age, Swedish uses “Jag är ... år.” The word “år” means “years old” in this context.
Phone numbers are usually read digit by digit. Practice them slowly first and then at a more natural speed.

legacyResources.summary: This lesson has been expanded so numbers become usable in real life: age, phone numbers, prices, room numbers, and slow careful dictation.

sections.heading: Teaching focus
content: Numbers are not only vocabulary; they are listening training. Learners often know the numbers on paper but freeze when they hear them quickly. Move between reading, hearing, and saying them.
Work especially with age and phone numbers, because those force you to pronounce digits clearly one by one and notice Swedish rhythm.

sections.heading: Common mistakes to watch
list: Do not rush teen numbers. Check carefully that you hear and say them distinctly.
When giving a phone number, say the digits clearly in groups instead of one long stream.
Mix recognition and production: first listen and identify, then say your own examples.

legacyCompanion.title: Countries, languages, and nationalities
legacyCompanion.goal: Name a few countries, languages, and nationalities in Swedish.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: You will connect country names with the languages people speak and practice short identity sentences.
This lesson helps you talk about where people come from and what languages they speak in a more natural way.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: After “Jag talar ...” use the language name, for example “Jag talar engelska.” Nationalities often change form depending on gender and number, so start by recognizing them.
A simple beginner pattern is: country with “kommer från”, language with “talar”, and nationality with “är”.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.english: Which language do you speak?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Jag talar engelska och lite svenska.

dialogue.english: Where are you from?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.english: I come from India.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.english: Do you also speak Hindi?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Ja, och jag lär mig svenska.
dialogue.english: Yes, and I am learning Swedish.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Say three languages you know or study.
Make one sentence with “Jag talar ...”.
Practice “lite svenska” for natural rhythm.
Read the dialogue until it feels smooth.

sections.heading: Extra practice ideas
list: Make three identity sentences: one with a country, one with a language, and one with a nationality.
Practice the contrast between “svenska” the language and “svensk” the nationality.

exercises.prompt: Match the idea to the right Swedish pattern

legacyResources.summary: This lesson now pushes the learner to build full identity sentences with country, language, and nationality information instead of naming isolated words.

sections.heading: Teaching focus
content: At this stage, the important skill is combining facts: where you come from, where you live, what language you speak, and what language you are learning. That creates a useful self-introduction block.
Teach country names and language names together, because learners often remember one without the other. Recycle them in the same sentence pattern several times.

sections.heading: Common mistakes to watch
list: Do not stop at one-word answers like Sverige or engelska. Always grow them into full sentences.
Notice the difference between a country and a language word. They are related, but not the same form.
Repeat the sentence frame with several countries so the pattern becomes flexible.

sections.heading: Guided practice
list: Introduce yourself with country, home city, and languages you speak.
Make three new sentences by changing only the country and language words.
Ask another person Varifrån kommer du? and Vilka språk talar du?

legacyCompanion.title: Verb är: to be
legacyCompanion.goal: Use the verb är in basic statements and questions.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: This lesson gives you one of the most important verbs in Swedish so you can describe identity, location, and simple facts.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: The present form is “är” for all persons: jag är, du är, vi är. Swedish does not change it like English does with am / is / are.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.english: Are you a student?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.english: Yes, I am a student.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.english: Are you tired today?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.english: A little, but I am fine.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Make three “Jag är ...” sentences.
Ask one yes/no question with “Är du ...?”
Replace “student” with your own role.
Read the dialogue with clear stress on “är”.

legacyResources.summary: This lesson now treats är as a sentence backbone: identity, description, and simple yes-no questions built from the same small structure.

sections.heading: Teaching focus
content: A beginner should overlearn är because it appears everywhere: names, nationality, feelings, descriptions, and simple classification. The goal is fast accurate use, not grammar theory alone.
Practice both statements and questions side by side. When the learner can switch between Du är trött. and Är du trött? the structure starts to become active.

sections.heading: Common mistakes to watch
list: Do not confuse Jag är bra with Jag mår bra. Use är for identity or description, and mår for how you feel.
Keep the word order stable when forming questions with är.
Avoid overtranslating from English. Use short natural Swedish sentences first.

sections.heading: Guided practice
list: Make five sentences with är about yourself, your city, and your family.
Turn each sentence into a yes-no question.
Answer the questions with both yes and no responses.

legacyCompanion.title: Simple sentence order
legacyCompanion.goal: Build short Swedish statements with subject + verb + extra information.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: You now practice the default Swedish word order so your beginner sentences sound stable and clear.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: A safe beginner pattern is subject + verb + object/place/time: “Jag läser svenska hemma.” Keep that pattern until it feels automatic.

dialogue.speaker: B

dialogue.speaker: B

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Write two sentences using subject + verb + place.

legacyResources.summary: This lesson has been strengthened into a sentence-building workshop so the learner understands that Swedish meaning depends heavily on keeping the parts in the right order.

sections.heading: Teaching focus
content: For early Swedish, sentence control matters more than long vocabulary lists. The learner should feel that a simple sentence has a dependable skeleton: subject first, verb second, then the rest.
Use familiar vocabulary while training order. That way the learner focuses on structure instead of fighting new words at the same time.

sections.heading: Common mistakes to watch
list: Do not drop the verb. Even a very short Swedish sentence normally needs a clear finite verb.
Do not pile up words without structure. Build from small complete sentences first.
Read your sentences aloud, because spoken rhythm often shows whether the order feels natural.

sections.heading: Guided practice
list: Build five short sentences from old vocabulary: person + verb + place or time.
Replace one part in each sentence while keeping the order stable.
Read the final five sentences aloud twice.

legacyCompanion.title: Likes and dislikes
legacyCompanion.goal: Say what you like and do not like in Swedish.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: Today you add opinions to your Swedish so you can talk about food, hobbies, and language learning preferences.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: Use “Jag gillar ...” for “I like ...” and “Jag gillar inte ...” for “I do not like ...”. The negation comes after the verb.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.english: Do you like Swedish music?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.english: Yes, I like Swedish music.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.english: Do you like tea?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.english: No, I do not like tea.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
list: Say three things you like.
Say two things you do not like.
Practice the difference between “gillar” and “gillar inte”.
Answer the dialogue with your real preferences.

legacyResources.summary: This lesson now develops opinions more carefully so the learner can say not only what they like, but also give a small reason and contrast.

sections.heading: Teaching focus
content: Likes and dislikes are high-value speaking material because they connect easily to food, hobbies, studies, places, and people. The learner should practice full opinion sentences, not just gillar or gillar inte.
A strong beginner pattern is opinion plus reason: Jag gillar kaffe eftersom det är gott. That turns a basic A1 answer into a more useful A2-style response.

sections.heading: Common mistakes to watch
list: Do not answer only with Ja or Nej when the topic is personal preference.
Remember that gillar often needs an object: Jag gillar musik, not only Jag gillar.
Use one reason word such as eftersom to make the answer more informative.

sections.heading: Guided practice
list: Give three likes and three dislikes with short reasons.
Compare two things: Jag gillar te men jag gillar inte kaffe.
Ask another person what they like and answer in a full sentence.

vocabulary.exampleSwedish: Jag gillar svenska eftersom språket är fint.
vocabulary.exampleEnglish: I like Swedish because the language is beautiful.

content: A very useful pattern is “Jag skulle vilja ha ...” for a polite “I would like ...”, but “Jag vill ha ...” is acceptable at beginner level.

sections.heading: Teaching focus
content: The target is smooth service interaction: greeting, ordering, adding one detail, and finishing politely. Learners should hear the café as a predictable script they can control.
Train set phrases in full chunks, especially Jag skulle vilja ha ... and Kan jag få ... because those patterns transfer to many public situations.

sections.heading: Common mistakes to watch
list: Do not point and say only one noun. Practice full order sentences.
Remember the social frame: greeting first, thanks at the end.
Be ready for a follow-up question such as something to drink or eat.

sections.heading: Teaching focus
content: Months become easier when tied to real personal information. Ask about birthdays, holidays, and important dates so the learner hears the month words in meaningful sentences.

sections.heading: Common mistakes to watch
list: Do not learn month names in isolation only. Use them inside complete date phrases.
Practice both asking and answering date questions.
Revisit ordinal-style dates regularly so they become automatic.

list: Say today's date and your birthday in Swedish.

legacyCompanion.title: Modal verbs
legacyCompanion.goal: Use can, must, want to, and may in simple statements.

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: Modal verbs let you speak about ability, obligation, and desire, which makes your Swedish much more functional.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: After a modal verb like “kan”, “vill”, or “måste”, the next verb stays in the infinitive: “Jag kan tala.” “Jag vill gå.”

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.english: Can you help me?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Ja, men jag måste gå snart.
dialogue.english: Yes, but I have to go soon.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.english: Yes, of course.

list: Make one sentence with each modal verb.

legacyResources.summary: This lesson now strengthens modal verbs as conversation tools for ability, necessity, permission, and desire rather than as isolated grammar labels.

sections.heading: Teaching focus
content: Modal verbs unlock practical communication quickly. With kan, vill, måste, and får, learners can handle many real needs even with limited vocabulary.
The key teaching point is chunking: modal plus infinitive. Repeat the pattern often until it feels automatic.

sections.heading: Common mistakes to watch
list: Do not forget the second verb after the modal when the meaning needs one.
Separate the meanings clearly: can, want, must, and may are not interchangeable.
Use personal examples so the verbs feel useful, not abstract.

sections.heading: Guided practice
list: Say three things you can do, three things you want to do, and two things you must do.
Ask another person what they can or want to do.
Make one polite permission question with får.

content: A practical beginner future form is “ska” + infinitive: “Jag ska studera.” It often means “am going to.”

sections.heading: Teaching focus
content: Future language becomes useful when it answers three questions at once: what, when, and why. Even a simple ska sentence becomes stronger with one time phrase and one detail.

sections.heading: Common mistakes to watch
list: Do not stop at Jag ska ... with no completion. Finish the action clearly.

sections.heading: Balansen (Textbook page 52)
content: Marias jobb är inte välbetalt men det är roligt. “Man presterar inte om man inte gillar jobbet”, brukar hon säga. Hon tycker också att hennes mentala hälsa är viktig och därför vill hon inte ha ett stressigt jobb. Hon är nöjd med sitt trygga jobb på en statlig myndighet och hon lär sina barn att pengar inte kan köpa allt i livet. Maria brukar säga att hennes man Peter är arbetsnarkoman eftersom han inte slutar med jobbet när han kommer hem. På sitt tidigare jobb hade han en giftig arbetsmiljö så han blev tvungen att säga upp sig. Efter detta startade han eget och därför jobbar han så mycket. Det är inte lätt att vara entreprenör! Han tänker på jobbet hela tiden. Maria tycker att det inte är bra för hälsan. “Det var bättre när han var arbetslös”, säger hon till Lena.

content: B1 tasks sometimes use numbers or trends, and many learners freeze when speaking about them.

sections.heading: Can-do targets
list: I can describe simple changes in numbers.
I can compare figures without overcomplicating the language.
I can mention approximate amounts clearly.

table.Example English: The price has increased a lot.

table.Example Swedish: Det är stor skillnad mellan åren.
table.Example English: There is a big difference between the years.
It costs approximately one hundred euros.
The share rose by ten percent.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: Keep it simple: level, change, comparison, possible reason.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.english: How do you see the numbers?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: Det verkar som att kostnaderna har ökat medan användningen har minskat lite.
dialogue.english: It seems that the costs have increased while the usage has decreased a little.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.english: Is the difference big?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.english: Yes, fairly big actually.

content: Use softeners: “jag är inte helt säker”, “jag ser det lite annorlunda”, “kanske beror det på ...”.

dialogue.speaker: B

sections.heading: Lesson focus
content: Hypothetical language often appears in speaking prompts and lets you show flexible thinking at B1.

table.Example Swedish: Om jag kunde skulle jag resa mer.
table.Example English: If I could, I would travel more.

table.Example Swedish: Jag skulle välja det andra alternativet.
table.Example English: I would choose the other option.

table.Example English: That would be a good opportunity.

sections.heading: Grammar note
content: A practical B1 frame is “Om jag hade mer tid skulle jag ...”, but simpler “om ... så ...” answers are also fine.

dialogue.english: I would rest first and then study some Swedish calmly.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.swedish: Och om du hade mer pengar?
dialogue.english: And if you had more money?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.swedish: I så fall skulle jag resa oftare.
dialogue.english: In that case I would travel more often.

grammarTopics.title: Swedish vowels, stress, and intelligibility
grammarTopics.summary: Focus on Å, Ä, Ö, vowel length, and the rhythm that makes beginner Swedish easier to understand.
rules: Train mouth shape, not only spelling.
Keep common chunks like “Jag mår bra” as sound units.
Short and long vowel differences can change meaning quickly.

grammarTopics.title: Pronouns and the highest-frequency verbs
grammarTopics.summary: Control of “jag, du, han, hon, vi, ni, de” plus verbs like vara, ha, göra, gå is essential for fluency.
rules: Learn pronoun + verb together in short phrases.
Use “jag heter”, “jag bor”, “jag har”, “jag tycker” as reusable frames.
Spoken “dom” often replaces written “de/dem”.

grammarTopics.title: Noun gender, articles, and basic noun phrases
grammarTopics.summary: Swedish nouns are easier when learned as full chunks with article and adjective, not as isolated words.
rules: Memorize “en/ett + noun” together.
Notice definite forms such as “bilen”, “köket”, “lägenheten”.
Adjectives change form depending on the noun phrase.

grammarTopics.title: Present tense for routines and facts
grammarTopics.summary: Present tense is the base for talking about routine, work, study, and future plans with time words.
rules: Most present forms are stable and reusable after a short period of drilling.
Combine present tense with time phrases early.
High-frequency verbs should become automatic in speech.

grammarTopics.title: Questions and verb-second word order
grammarTopics.summary: Swedish relies heavily on the verb-second principle, especially after time and place phrases.
rules: In main clauses the verb usually comes second.
Questions and reordered sentences still keep a clear structure.
Practice V2 inside useful patterns, not as an abstract rule only.

examples.english: In the morning I study Swedish.

grammarTopics.title: Modal verbs and polite request frames
grammarTopics.summary: Kan, vill, skulle, måste, får, and bör are central for service encounters, permissions, and rules.
rules: Use modals to soften requests and clarify obligation.
Polite forms matter more than complex grammar in real service talk.
Contrast permission, necessity, and preference clearly.

examples.swedish: Jag skulle vilja boka en tid.
examples.english: I would like to book an appointment.

grammarTopics.title: Past tense for everyday narration
grammarTopics.summary: Past tense lets you explain events, routines from yesterday, and practical problems in time order.
rules: Start with the most frequent past forms and high-value chunks.
Sequence markers often matter more than perfect verb accuracy.
Past tense and perfect tense serve different functions; train both.

grammarTopics.title: Perfect tense for experience and present relevance
grammarTopics.summary: Perfect tense is useful for biography, work experience, and integration-related topics.
rules: Use har + supine for completed actions linked to the present.
Pair perfect tense with “redan”, “ännu”, and duration phrases.
Distinguish between life experience and one finished past event.

examples.swedish: Jag har bott i Finland i tre år.
examples.english: I have lived in Finland for three years.
I have already sent the email.

grammarTopics.title: Future meaning, intentions, and planning
grammarTopics.summary: Swedish future meaning often stays simple and practical through time words and modal expressions.
rules: Present tense plus time word is often enough.
Use ska and tänker for clearer intention when needed.
Planning answers should include sequence and reason.

examples.english: I intend to apply for the course.

grammarTopics.title: Connectors and subordinate clauses
grammarTopics.summary: Connected B1 Swedish depends on common linking words more than on advanced grammar terminology.
rules: Use because, when, if, although, and therefore actively.
Check word order after opening clauses.
Connected sentences should still stay short enough to control.

examples.swedish: När jag kommer hem lagar jag mat.
examples.english: When I come home I cook.

examples.swedish: Jag stannade hemma eftersom jag var sjuk.
examples.english: I stayed home because I was sick.

grammarTopics.title: Comparison, opinion, and recommendation language
grammarTopics.summary: B1 answers become stronger when comparison and opinion phrases are easy to access.
rules: Compare first, then judge or recommend.
Support opinions with at least one reason and one example.
Softened disagreement sounds more natural than direct contradiction.

examples.swedish: Det här alternativet är bättre eftersom det är billigare.
examples.english: This option is better because it is cheaper.

grammarTopics.title: Formal and semi-formal writing patterns
grammarTopics.summary: Practical emails, requests, and short official texts are high-return preparation for YKI writing.
rules: State reason, context, request, and closing clearly.
One idea per sentence is often enough.
Leave time to check task completion and tone.

examples.english: I am writing regarding my application.

examples.swedish: Jag vore tacksam för ett svar.
examples.english: I would be grateful for a response.

grammarTopics.title: YKI task strategies for reading, listening, speaking, and writing
grammarTopics.summary: Retrieval practice, note control, timed output, and post-task review matter as much as new vocabulary in the final stretch.
rules: Predict topic before listening or reading.
Answer the task directly before adding extra detail.
Reuse strong structures rather than chasing rare words under pressure.

grammarTopics.title: Vowels and pronunciation
grammarTopics.summary: Your notes show that vowel quality is a core A1 skill. Mouth shape and vowel length change meaning quickly in Swedish.
rules: A, O, U, Y, I, E, Ö, Ä, Å each need a distinct mouth position.
Long vowel + short consonant often contrasts with short vowel + long consonant.
Minimal pairs such as tack / tak and ful / full are worth repeating aloud.
grammarTopics.sourceLabel: Analyzed class notes from Apr 15 to May 9, 2026, plus Learn Swedish Lab reading extracts, the Swedish A1-A2 tutorial, and a teacher-led lesson expansion from May 18, 2026

grammarTopics.title: Sound changes before front vowels
grammarTopics.summary: Several Swedish consonants soften or shift before front vowels like y, i, e, ö, and ä.
rules: G before y/i/e/ö/ä often sounds like a soft j.
K before y/i/e/ö/ä often sounds like tj.
sk before y/i/e/ö/ä often sounds like sh.
hj, dj, and lj often lose the first letter at the beginning of a word.
grammarTopics.sourceLabel: Analyzed class notes from Apr 15 to May 9, 2026, plus Learn Swedish Lab reading extracts, the Swedish A1-A2 tutorial, and a teacher-led lesson expansion from May 18, 2026

grammarTopics.title: Personal pronouns
grammarTopics.summary: The notes reinforce the full beginner pronoun set and the spoken form dom for de.
rules: Use jag, du, han, hon, vi, ni, de in writing.
In speech, de is very often pronounced dom.
grammarTopics.sourceLabel: Analyzed class notes from Apr 15 to May 9, 2026, plus Learn Swedish Lab reading extracts, the Swedish A1-A2 tutorial, and a teacher-led lesson expansion from May 18, 2026

grammarTopics.title: Question words
grammarTopics.summary: Your notes provide the high-frequency question words needed for A1 conversation.
rules: Use vad for what, var for where, hur for how, varför for why, and när for when.
In direct questions, the verb usually stays before the subject unless a question word already starts the sentence.
grammarTopics.sourceLabel: Analyzed class notes from Apr 15 to May 9, 2026, plus Learn Swedish Lab reading extracts, the Swedish A1-A2 tutorial, and a teacher-led lesson expansion from May 18, 2026

grammarTopics.title: Verb-second word order
grammarTopics.summary: The most repeated rule in your notes is the golden V2 rule: the finite verb stays in second position.
rules: The first position can be a person, time, or place chunk.
The finite verb still stays second even when a time or place moves to the front.
The subject stays next to the finite verb, either before or after it.

examples.swedish: Jag ska baka en kaka ikväll.
examples.english: I am going to bake a cake tonight.

examples.swedish: Ikväll ska jag baka en kaka.
examples.english: Tonight I am going to bake a cake.

grammarTopics.sourceLabel: Analyzed class notes from Apr 15 to May 9, 2026, plus Learn Swedish Lab reading extracts, the Swedish A1-A2 tutorial, and a teacher-led lesson expansion from May 18, 2026

grammarTopics.title: Modal and helper verbs
grammarTopics.summary: Your notes give a practical helper-verb system: kan, måste, vill, ska, brukar, hinner, and orkar.
rules: After a helper verb, the next verb normally stays in the infinitive.
Brukar expresses habit, while ska expresses plans.
Hinner is about available time; orkar is about energy or strength.

examples.english: I do not have the energy to study more.

grammarTopics.sourceLabel: Analyzed class notes from Apr 15 to May 9, 2026, plus Learn Swedish Lab reading extracts, the Swedish A1-A2 tutorial, and a teacher-led lesson expansion from May 18, 2026

grammarTopics.title: Negation and adverb placement
grammarTopics.summary: Inte, också, alltid, ofta, sällan, and aldrig behave like adverbials and often share the same slot in the sentence.
rules: In simple main clauses, inte usually comes after the finite verb and subject.
Också and many frequency adverbs often use the same position as inte.
Ibland can stand first in the sentence or later in the sentence, but not directly before the object in the wrong place.

examples.english: I do not want to eat pizza.

examples.swedish: Jag vill också köpa en banan.
examples.english: I also want to buy a banana.

examples.swedish: Jag går alltid på gymmet efter jobbet.
examples.english: I always go to the gym after work.

grammarTopics.sourceLabel: Analyzed class notes from Apr 15 to May 9, 2026, plus Learn Swedish Lab reading extracts, the Swedish A1-A2 tutorial, and a teacher-led lesson expansion from May 18, 2026

grammarTopics.title: Noun gender and definite form
grammarTopics.summary: Your notes combine en/ett basics with definite noun endings and when to use the definite form.
rules: Most Swedish nouns are common gender en nouns; a smaller group are ett nouns.
The definite form usually adds the ending to the noun: boken, jobbet, mötet.
Use the definite form when both people know which thing you mean, much like English the.

examples.swedish: Jag hade en tuff dag på jobbet.
examples.english: I had a tough day at work.

grammarTopics.sourceLabel: Analyzed class notes from Apr 15 to May 9, 2026, plus Learn Swedish Lab reading extracts, the Swedish A1-A2 tutorial, and a teacher-led lesson expansion from May 18, 2026

grammarTopics.title: Adjective agreement
grammarTopics.summary: Your notes give the full A1 adjective pattern: base form for en nouns, -t for ett nouns, and -a for plural and definite forms.
rules: Use the base adjective with en nouns: en rolig dag.
Add -t with ett nouns when needed: ett roligt jobb.
Use the plural-like -a form in plural and definite contexts: roliga filmer, den nya bilen, min nya bil.
grammarTopics.sourceLabel: Analyzed class notes from Apr 15 to May 9, 2026, plus Learn Swedish Lab reading extracts, the Swedish A1-A2 tutorial, and a teacher-led lesson expansion from May 18, 2026

grammarTopics.title: Plural patterns
grammarTopics.summary: The notes add useful A1 plural patterns and reminder examples for both indefinite and definite plural forms.
rules: Plural endings vary by noun group, so learn common words with their plural forms.
The definite plural works like English the + plural, for example bilarna and filmerna.
Some common words have irregular plurals, such as vän / vänner.
grammarTopics.sourceLabel: Analyzed class notes from Apr 15 to May 9, 2026, plus Learn Swedish Lab reading extracts, the Swedish A1-A2 tutorial, and a teacher-led lesson expansion from May 18, 2026

grammarTopics.title: Numbers, dates, and time
grammarTopics.summary: Your notes add number pronunciation, ordinal dates, and Swedish-style half-hour expressions.
rules: Dates are often spoken with an ordinal value: den 10:e maj.
Swedish halv points to the next hour, so halv sex means 5:30.
Use klockan for clock time and datum for calendar date.

examples.english: The meeting starts at five on the dot.

grammarTopics.sourceLabel: Analyzed class notes from Apr 15 to May 9, 2026, plus Learn Swedish Lab reading extracts, the Swedish A1-A2 tutorial, and a teacher-led lesson expansion from May 18, 2026

grammarTopics.title: Job phrases and workplace prepositions
grammarTopics.summary: The notes clarify how professions and workplaces are expressed in natural beginner Swedish.
rules: Do not add an article after job titles in simple statements: jag jobbar som lärare.
Use på with many workplaces and institutions: på en bank, på ett universitet, på Nokia.
Use hemifrån for working from home and på distans for remote work.
grammarTopics.sourceLabel: Analyzed class notes from Apr 15 to May 9, 2026, plus Learn Swedish Lab reading extracts, the Swedish A1-A2 tutorial, and a teacher-led lesson expansion from May 18, 2026

grammarTopics.title: Preteritum (past tense)
grammarTopics.summary: Your notes introduce the past tense through groups, irregular forms, and diary-style practice.
rules: Many verbs build the past from the base form plus -de or -te, but common verbs can be irregular.
Start with high-frequency irregulars such as var, gick, gjorde, såg, hade, and kom.
Past-time markers like igår and förra veckan make the tense easier to recognize and produce.

examples.english: I talked with the boss yesterday.

examples.swedish: Vi åkte till Italien förra året.
examples.english: We went to Italy last year.

examples.swedish: Jag vaknade sent och åt pizza.
examples.english: I woke up late and ate pizza.

grammarTopics.title: Som as a relative pronoun
grammarTopics.summary: The notes introduce som for joining two sentences into one smoother noun description.
rules: Use som to refer back to the noun before it, much like who, which, or that in English.
Som can also mean like / such as, but that is a different pattern from the relative use.

examples.swedish: Jag har en syster som är veterinär.
examples.english: I have a sister who is a veterinarian.

examples.swedish: Han spelar ett datorspel som han fick i present.
examples.english: He is playing a video game that he got as a present.

grammarTopics.title: Hem, hemma, and hemifrån
grammarTopics.summary: Your notes distinguish location, movement toward home, and movement from home very clearly.
rules: Use hemma for location without movement.
Use hem for movement toward home.
Use hemifrån for movement from home or working from home.

grammarTopics.title: Health phrases
grammarTopics.summary: The health notes are built around reliable chunks that work immediately in everyday situations.
rules: Use Jag har ont i + definite body part to describe pain.
For appointments, use Jag har tid hos ... or Jag har läkartid.
Words like förkyld, feber, and hostar are good A1 survival vocabulary.

examples.english: I have an appointment with the doctor.

examples.swedish: Jag är förkyld och har feber.
examples.english: I have a cold and a fever.

grammarTopics.title: Weather patterns
grammarTopics.summary: The notes give the standard weather sentence frames used in everyday Swedish.
rules: Use Det är + adjective for conditions like varmt, kallt, and mulet.
Use Det regnar, Det snöar, and Det blåser for common weather events.
Add temperature with Det är ... grader.
